ResponsesInList.Text: Tim, this kind of behaviour is not limited to Moodle but to most commercial LMS systems we have had experience with as well.  to get around this kind of thing, it is usually up to the SCO/course itself to communicate with the LMS periodically, to keep the users session alive. we typically create our courses/sco object with a 3 - 5 minute "ping" to the server , thereby preventing the type of situation you experienced.  for our clients we never know how their servers are setup from a session time-out perspective,  most systems default to 15 or 30 minutes. so we set the course up to make a communication request in the background of every 3 -5 minutes to keep the session alive.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle behaviour if session times out while SCO is open
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Burke, I've resolved the Tim's problem implementing a pulser on the lms (not in moodle but other opensource lms). Your solution looks great and I was wondering if you can tell us more about. What do you ping exactly? Do you use SCORM api calls? Thanks in advance. Ciao Marco

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle behaviour if session times out while SCO is open
ResponsesInList.Text: Marco, we usually just make a call to to the SCORM API to send current "bookmarking" type data to the LMS.  to could do any kind of call you want, a "get" or "put"  as long as the system is hitting the LMS, it will not terminate the session.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle behaviour if session times out while SCO is open
ResponsesInList.Text: In our experience with various LMS applications, the way the SCORM API was written is that all data is contained withing the API once it is loaded. This means a get or put only hits the API itself and there is no communication with the server. But if you issue a "commit" then all data currently in the API is sent to the server. The Moodle API looks like it written this way. When the API is created for the course, all data is included. So all "get" commands are actually only reading data from local variables, and all "put" commands are updating only local variables. It is not until the "commit" command is executed is the data actually sent to the server.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle behaviour if session times out while SCO is open
ResponsesInList.Text: This is correct with Moodle mod/scorm. Inorder to force a round trip to the server you need to invoke a Commit() (SCORM 2004) or LMSCommit() (SCORM 1.2). Cheers, Piers Harding.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM display wait time issues on Moodle 1.93
ResponsesInList.Text: John, if you look in the application files at moodle\htdocs\mod\scorm\loadSCO.php around line of that file you will see a variable getting defined named "$delayseconds"  it is being set to 2 seconds.  this code is used to allow the browser time to locate location of the SCO API calls needed for the SCO object to communicate back to the server so it can report completion status, grades, etc. You can try adjusting this value to a lower number say 1. or .5  but it may cause some issues with the content being able to get a handle on the API  and being able to effectively communicate back.  This type of delay is fairly common in most commercial LMS systems.  You could also modify the on screen information of this file or the gif that is loaded to be more "entertaining"  or to communicate more clearly why their is a wait. you can locate the animated gif in your "theme" directory moodle\htdocs\theme\{your theme} then go to pix\mod\scorm\pix  and rplace the wait.gif  with one of your choice maybe something like this http://gifsrus.110mb.com/cartoon/line-figures1/2-Ninja-150x100.gif

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM display wait time issues on Moodle 1.93
ResponsesInList.Text: the timing is going to be more relative to the end users computer. the way the scorm api works, which is different from the older AICC api,  is the courses do not care where the server is, they simply look in the "windows" that lunahced the course to find the API to communicate with.  it typcially first looks at itself, then its parent window and that parent's parent window and so on  until it finds the API or runs out of parent windows to check. the older AICC API had hte course talking directly to the server, via URL reference that was passed to the launched course.  in SCORM the LMS  is soley responsible for communicating with the server,  and the course is responsible for finding the code in the LMS window and communicates only with that. long story short, it just depends  and i imagine the moodle developers landed on 2 seconds from doing some testing or getting feedback from the community and determine this is the shortest but safest time to wait for allof that "checking" to take place.  you may find in your environment you can reduce it,  but leaving it at 2 seconds and simply modifying the content of the loading page, or even simpler the animated gif  would be the safest way to go. if your environment is public college then the animated gif could be related to a beer drinking game, that should hold their attention

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM display wait time issues on Moodle 1.93
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi there, Just confirming that everyone is correct - the delay is there to allow the SCORM api to load in the browser. the Delay has always been there, however in 1.9.3 we've added a "message" to notify the user that something is happening and to prevent impatient users from reloading the page during the delay. Some browsers load this quicker than others ( IE has traditionally been the worst offender) - I have heard suggestions of adding a check during the delay to see if the API has loaded already and if so, shorten the delay. Piers and I would be happy to review any code that performed this, and would be more than happy to get such a patch into core.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM display wait time issues on Moodle 1.93
ResponsesInList.Text: What I was saying was that if a developer spent some time looking at a way to check to see if the full api has loaded that is cross-browser compatible that loads quicker than just forcing to wait the fixed time period. Piers and I(the core SCORM Module Maintainers) would be happy to review any such code for inclusion in Moodle core. The time delay is not for your "servers" benefit, but for the users local browser to load the Javascript API correctly before allowing the SCORM object to make any SCORM calls - if the javascript has not been loaded completely in the browser, and the SCORM object makes a call to the API it will fail and will throw a range of errors, and no user data will be saved. Also, this check/time delay has always been in SCORM, all that we have done recently in 1.9.3 is add some notification to the user that it is happening to prevent them from getting "bored" and trying to refresh the browser. I'm not sure what you mean by "the API check" ? - I'm guessing you may have misunderstood my initial post? - there is currently no "plan" to work on such a change to the javascript, however if someone else spent the time on it, as I mention above, we'd be happy to look at/review any code that they might provide.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to incorporate Articulate QuizMaker into Moodle's Scorm?
ResponsesInList.Text: Just a few advantages of the quiz module over a Flash-based quiz such as Quizmaker: With the flash quiz, if a change is made to a question or answer, the project must be republished and will not take effect until this occures. Also, if you use the SCORM import process to overwrite the previous version, all records are lost. With the quiz module, you must simply make the change and it will be effective immediately. You may also regrade prior attempts based on a change to the correct answer. With the flash quiz, there is no way to see the actual test that was presented to the student. With the quiz module, you can see historical attempts and answers given by each student. As stated before, these attempts may be regraded if the answers to questions are changed. With Quizmaker, your questions exist in the quiz project itself. If you desire to create multiple tests, you must duplicate that quiz project creating more work if you need to make a change or revision to questions. Also, you may not create subcategories within a project for an "end of course quiz". With the quiz module, you may created multiple subcategories and create category-specific quizzes and quizzes which sample multiple categories. In the flash quiz, a random quiz can be generated, but there is no way to guarantee that the student receives certain "required" questions. The quiz module allows you to select a specified number of random questions in addition to any required questions. The random question will not repeat the required questions. Finally, there is no way to track statistics using flash-based quizzes since the only element stored is the score. The quiz module provides historical data which can be used to further improve your questions and the organization of those questions into categories of difficulty if desired. These categories can then be used to develop consistent testing when using randomized questions. I hope this helps anyone who reads this. Jamie

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: One more consideration about Quizmaker
ResponsesInList.Text: If you have Excel, it will be very easy. All of the Quizmaker files are text-based and tab-delimited. I used the GIFT format for importing questions into the Quiz module. The help file is attached to this posting. You'll notice that the format is not that different from the Quizmaker files. You'll need to simply paste the copied questions from the Quizmaker file opened with Notepad (Question/Answer rows only) into Excel. Excel with divide the rows into cells. You'll then be able to quickly go through and reformat each set of answers to conform to the GIFT standard as shown in the help file. One thing to pay attention to is where you have multiple correct answers (multiple selection). You'll need to attach a percentage for each of the correct answers so that Moodle will grade appropriately. (The quiz module gives partial credit for multiple selection questions when only a portion of the correct answers are selected.) All of the correct responses percentages should add up to 100%. For correct percentage numbers, see below. Percentages understood by the quiz module for multiple selection answers are as follows: (Negative numbers may also be specified to penalize for incorrect answers given.) 5,10,14.2857,16.666,20,25,30,33.333,40,50,60,66.666,70,75,80,90,100 Also, regarding the use of graphics, the Quizmaker question row will also contain the file name of the graphic used. This will be very helpful when importing the picture into the Quiz module. (This will have to be done after importing all of your questions through the normal question editing process. So, make a list of the questions containing graphics so that you can go back and add those after importing.) Good luck with this and let me know if you have any more questions. I don't think you'll regret switching over.

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi.  I am examining Moodle as an alternative LMS for administering SCORM-based exams.  I am currently using SCORM modules created with QW3 (a nice commercial package) on Ecampus, formerly WebCT.  It works OK but the SCORM package in Ecampus does not support IP address filtering except for their assessment package.  SCORMs must be run unfiltered.  This causes a real hassle as we have proctored labs for the exam, and want to preclude students taking the exams outside the labs.  We can track where they take it in the QW3 results, but then it is an enforcement issue So does Moodle allow SCORMs to be filtered for IP address?  I installed 1.8 and noted there was a quiz package with IP filtering but that the SCORM resource didn't seem to have this.  Moodle seems fairly similar to Ecampus, albeit a bit spartan Is there a WIKI somewhere which covers the three things I would like to do a) enroll students with password authentication b) upload and set up scorms to selectively release with IP filtering c) do group management for selective release, scheduling, etc Thanks

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: using Moodle for SCORM administration
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Joseph, Moodle 1.9.3 passes all the SCORM 1.2 tests, and will hopefully at some point get official ADL SCORM Certification, but SCORM 2004 is not yet completely supported. So If you're using SCORM 2004, Moodle may not be the solution for you sorry! SCORM doesn't allow selective release via timeframes (which is actually a bug and should be fixed in the next month or so) - most other Core modules in Moodle do this, and it would be really easy to add this to SCORM Also - there's no functionality at this stage to allow IP restriction of SCORM objects, however it would be relatively easy to add this to SCORM as well. Feel free to create a Tracker item for it at tracker.moodle.org - If someone generated a patch for this against Moodle 1.9 and 2.0 I'd be happy to review it for inclusion in Moodle Core. But unfortunately for you it's not something that would sit high on Piers or my list. If both of these are something you would be willing to help fund development on, you could contract any developer to do the work, and we'd be happy to review it for inclusion in core, or you could contract a Moodle Partner to do the work for you. The easiest Moodle enrollment plugin to use is Email based self-registration - check out the docs here for info: http://docs.moodle.org/en/Email-based_self-registration However as anyone can create accounts on your site, this could potentially pose a spam risk on your site. Anyone could create an account and post "spam" on their profile or into any forum inside courses that you allow self-enrolment without an enrolment key. There are a range of Authentication methods, and enrolment methods you can use which will prevent this. in terms of Group management for selective release I presume you mean that you would like to release "SCORM object A" to Group 1 at x time, and "SCORM object A" to Group 2 at y time. This would be possible (if time selection was added) by having each group in a different course inside Moodle, and uploading the same object to each course. - it does mean duplication of your SCORM objects, but it might suit your requirements. hope that helps!

We get a lot of students (.250 a section). It seems odd to me that no one wants to add IP restriction to SCORM modules when it is typically available in native assessment modules. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tracking & reporting learner participation in SCORM content?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Greg, The SCORM reporting is a bit different then the normal Moodle Reporting. There are a couple of ways to get to the detailed data tracking. First, On the course summary page you will see a link to the right of the course name that says "View reports for X attempts". This will bring up a report basic information for all attempts for all users. To get additional detail you click on the attempt number for a user. This gives you a little more information along with a link "Track details". This gives you all the detailed data that the SCORM based course tracks. The second way of getting to the details is by going to a users profile and selecting Activity reports. Depending on where you do this from you may then have to select the course you want the report to be based on. Once you have the correct course you will notice a new menu directly under the tabs. You want Complete Report. Not exactly the most convenient way of getting to the data you want, but it works. We are in the process of designing our own report plug-in for the Grade Module and will share it once we have it complete. Ron

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tracking & reporting learner participation in SCORM content?
ResponsesInList.Text: You are absolutely correct, detail reporting is at the learner level only. This is why we are looking at creating our own SCORM report to plug into the Grade book module. Since we have only used the SCORM format I didn't realize that you wouldn't be able to see that link at the course level. I setup a course in a format like you have and found that the link can be found by either selecting SCORM/AICC in the Activities block, or within the course you can click on the SCORM activity and then on that screen you will see the "View reports for..." link. We did find a way of uploading a large course that had several SCOs in parts so as not to have to worry about the upload size limit. You can make several smaller packages out of all the SCOs and one master package with the IMSManifest file that points to all the SCOs. Then do the following: Create a SCORM formated course Upload the Master SCORM Package and choose this one to use as the SCORM course. Then go into the SCORM activity and select to Update ths SCORM/AICC Select the Choose or upload button again Navigate to the folder that was created for the SCORM activity. It should be a number. Upload all the other zip files you created and unzip them. The tricky part is making sure the folder structure is setup correctly. Close the window without Choosing a file, leaving the first one you selected as the package file to use. You should now have all the files uploaded for the large multi-sco course. Ron

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to create SCORM-compatible moodle site?
ResponsesInList.Text: SCORM is a standard for creating learning content objects--reusable blocks of learning, if you will. You don't create a SCORM-compatible Moodle site. Rather, you load SCORM content into Moodle. Moodle is a container for SCORM objects. It doesn't create SCORM objects itself. It just uses them.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Articulate Presenter 7, Godaddy, scorm import problems.
ResponsesInList.Text: Progress! (Bradley, thanks for your offer, but I think I've got the main issue resolved now - I might take you up later, if I may.) As I kept digging through references to this problem, it seemed to be related to filepaths and slash arguments. GoDaddy apparently runs php as a cgi process on shared linux server accounts which changes/limits some variables. I found a reference to a possible fix involving the use of the line cgi.fix_pathinfo = 1 in the user's local php.ini file. Tried it, but phpinfo.php still reported that cgi.fix_pathinfo was off. Finally realized that because I am running php5, I needed to put this line in a similar file entitled php5.ini. After doing so, the lesson window will now display and run the imported Presenter flash file. Also, a cursory review indicates that moodle is properly recognizing and scoring the embedded quiz in my sample presenter package. So far so good. It's really all I've had time to investigate today. A couple of quirks that I can see already: 1. The window that contains my Presenter flash presentation has a single quote mark leading off a blank line/space above the flash view. It's visually unappealing and more importantly wastes valuable space, causing the flash to shrink into the area below the top line/space. I saw this quote mark by itself before I got the flash to play (actually, it was a double quote mark at some point - no idea why it changed). I'm guessing this is an improper parsing of the code that calls the flash file, but don't know how to fix it. Any ideas, anyone? 2. Several posts have indicated that slashargs must be turned on in the moodle admin area (mine now is) and further, that the setting is forced on for scorm imports in recent versions of moodle, because it is required for scorm operations. When I run /moodle/admin/health.php I get an error report indicating that slashargs are turned on, but that nonetheless the slashargs test has failed. The above fix has resolved some problems, but I wonder if this issue means I will have incomplete/faulty operation of my scorm units. Does anyone know? GoDaddy is such a popular hosting site, I know a lot of folks are bumping into similar issues. So far I've been able to find workarounds for virutally all of their limitations. I hope some of the project gurus will continue to work on ways that sites hosted on shared servers can sucessfully run such a great looking project as moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: ICT 4 Life
ResponsesInList.Text: You know when someone comes along and says they got it work..... ....well I followed the instructions and it works! It just has the ActiveBook, none of the other stuff. Here is how I did it. Do an "Installing to workstation from a network" install. Third of the way down page 3. I stuck it into a folder on the C: Download the file from http://centraal.uk.knowledgebox.com/kbase/idx/88/197/article/ Follow the instructions - unzip into the folder "ActiveTeach 1" Run the Bat file "1_Prepare_VLE.bat" you have just unziped. Zip the CONTENTS of the "ActiveTeach 1" folder - NOT the whole folder - just what is inside. I then used ftp to send the resulting zip file to the Moodle box and put it in the backupdata folder of the course so I could find it again. Saved me having to change the upload limit. Then got Moodle to add an activity - SCORM Job done Running 1.9.1+ (Build: 20080611) on a SUSE box

ResponsesInList.Text: We have a corporate client we are helping to implement Moodle with.  they need a very basic single course setup.  the course will have 7 scorm based modules and 1 scorm based exam. we set them up on the Front Page as activities , so users do not have to go through the step of enroling into the course. this all works perfect, except it appears that scorm based content does not report its AICC data into the database when launched from the Front Page.  the courses all work perfectly when launched from a course that is setup through add/edit courses.  but the same courses do not report their status when placed as activities on the Front Page.  the API's do not through any errors, but no data is ever written into the DB.  is ther ea hack we can make to allow this to take place?  the company really likes the simplicity of this approach, if we can simply get the activitiy reporting working properly. allowing users to access the grades for these lessons would also be a big bonus. as this does not seem to be available on the Front Page as well. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Scorm Activities on Front Page

ResponsesInList.Title: Changing course format to SCORM deletes course
ResponsesInList.Text: One of our tutors accidentally changed the format of a course to SCORM format and the course dissappeared completely, why did this happen and is there any way to restore it?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Changing course format to SCORM deletes course
ResponsesInList.Text: the SCORM course format is designed to allow a single SCORM object to be viewed/displayed. Changing your course to use the SCORM format doesn't delete anything from the course, however as it doesn't use topics or weeks any content previously added will be hidden. simply change the course format back to the Weekly or Topics format and you will probably see the old content viewable again.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No input file specified.
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi There, Scorm objects don't work with Slashargs disabled. - this is typically related to IIS servers and doesn't usually occur with Apache . Newer versions of PHP fixes this for IIS users. we have added a warning regarding this to the latest version of 1.8 and 1.9 that displays when you attempt to create a Scorm object when Slashargs is disabled. You can enable Slashargs in the admin settings > Server > HTTP - however enabling it may not work as your server may not support this. If Slasharguments is not supported on the server you are using, then SCORM objects won't work. edit* in fact - this post explains it quite well. http://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=36813#p457524

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No input file specified.
ResponsesInList.Text: Hey guys, I just install a new Moodle 1.9.2 on my server which have almost same specs that GoDaddy and there is no more problems of "No Input File Specified" of course I've to uncheck slasharguments on Server/ HTTP/ Please let me know if work for some other. Regards,

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No input file specified.
ResponsesInList.Text: if your server requires Slasharguments to be unchecked (disabled) SCORM objects will NOT work correctly as they require relative paths to work correctly. with the latest version of Moodle 1.9Stable and 1.8Stable, SCORM ignores the slasharguments setting and forces the use of slasharguments, as the other method does not work. This means that if your server does not support slasharguments, you will get the No input file specified error.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Zip or Unzip a SCORM file?
ResponsesInList.Text: The only problem that I've been able to provoke with this, is when the popup blocker interferes with the launching of the SCORM. You need to ensure that the popup blocker permanently lets your site through (temporarily enabling it isn't enough), and then relaunch the object. The 3 scenarios as I see it are: (1) SCORM launched in same window - no problem because there is no popup. (2) SCORM launched in a popup window - big problem if it is trapped by the popup blocker - it kills it dead. Site must be added as an exception and SCORM relaunched. (3) SCORM in an LMS - this is fine when it is launched as link target to a new window as this isnt treated the same as a JavaScript popup. Cheers, Piers Harding.

I find students quite like short Multi Choice quizzes, particularly if they are quite short (maybe 10 questions) and the questions are unambiguous. My subject is IT so it is quite suited to that type of Quiz. If your subject was English Literature quizzes might not be quite so handy.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Excuse my ignorance
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Paul, You're right "Scorm" is definately designed for single learner/self paced pump and dump type learning. Moodle however is not! - Moodle allows you to use Scorm objects, but it is really just one of the tools inside Moodle. Many things that can be accomplished via a scorm object can be accomplished using the tools inside moodle itself - eg quiz/multiple choice etc... and a larger range of tools that wouldn't sit inside a Scorm object are available like, forums, wikis, chats, assignment submission etc etc. Moodle is used in a very large range of Higer Education institutions where it supports on-campus delivery of subjects and group based learning, as well as many many other applications! in fact - of the people who have filled out this choice: http://moodle.org/mod/choice/view.php?id=158 Universities account for the largest percentage of where people are using Moodle! Hope that helps! Dan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM module: Possible bug: Re-setting lesson status after completed
ResponsesInList.Text: For those of you using Articulate Presenter 5.2, Articulate has published a workaround on their support site here . Unfortunately, when I applied this, it would indeed maintain completion status for already-completed SCORM lessons, but wouldn't update SCORM lessons with untried or incomplete status to indicate completion. So I did some digging and comparison of the original file and the workaround file and created a hybrid lms.js that specifically supports the needs of Moodlers. To install: follow the instructions in the above link, but use the attached lms.js instead of Articulate's version . Keep a backup of the original! To apply this to a published AP 5.2 SCORM module without republishing, you need to find the proper folder within MoodleData and copy the attached lms.js into it, replacing the existing file. Usually the location fo this file is <moodledata>/<c##>/moddata/scorm/<m##>/lms/ where <moodledata>, <c##>, and <m##> are the moodle data directory, the course directory (a number), and the SCORM object's directory (another number), respectively. Please note that if you re-publish your SCORM presentation, you will lose the custom lms.js unless you follow the steps in the above link to make it the default lms.js for all AP presentations. You can figure out if you're in the right directory by looking at <m##>/data/presentation. xml and looking for the original published filename in the metadata . I hope this turns out to be useful to some of you. PM me or reply if you have any questions - I'll do the best I can to answer them, even though I'm still relatively new to Moodle myself.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM : BUG : Review mode not working
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, SCORM LMS's are not intended to be judgemental on the SCO. It is the SCO's responsibility to set pass/fail/score. (Except for setting pass grade but even then the LMS will expect a score to be sent), That your SCORM communicates successfully with the SCORM module and sets status complete means your SCO sent a status complete or LMSFinish(). On review the SCO are not registering/interpreting the complete status and sending new data overwriting status. This is happening in preview mode, your SCO is not picking up the mode status as preview and writes data to the LMS as though it is running first time through.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Locking a SCORM zip
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Mary, When Moodle (and any LMS) imports a SCORM package it will unzip the file and put the contents somewhere. In Moodle the contents are put into the moddata/scorm directory inside the Moodle course you're working in. This means, in theory, that admins could go into that directory and edit the materials. So I see your problem. I see you have a number of possible approaches: 1) Cut down the number of Moodle installations and take control of them (why do you have several across the company?) 2) Reduce the capabilities of site administrators so they can't get into the course files area 3) Build the contents of the SCORM packages in such a way as to make them uneditable (eg. in Flash) What's the likelihood of the site admins doing that sort of editing? They'll need to be fairly technically adept even to find the materials. All the best, Mark

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How can I add math formula in Scorm package
ResponsesInList.Text: A SCORM package consists of some self-contained Web content that you create outside Moodle. Moodle merely "plays" the SCORM package. So if you have formulas written in LaTeX, Moodle will not render them, even if the TeX filter is turned on. How did you create your math quiz? Your SCORM package? Here's one possible way it could be done. Use ExamView to create a math quiz and export it as HTML. When you export, formulas in your test are saved as GIF images (the HTML pages have img tags that point to the images). Package the HTML and images in a SCORM package and upload it into Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM course scoring issues
ResponsesInList.Text: Chris, Find out from the developers what info is being sent to the LMS. If you have question pages what are the settings for how the lesson behaves when someone answers them. If it were me (and I may be talking above my pay grade here) I would use the SCORM authoring program to create these rules or set learning objectives. Otherwise, you have these Grading Methods in Moodle: Learning Objects This mode shows the number of completed/passed Learning Objects for the activity. The max value is the number of Package's Learning Objects. Highest grade The grade page will display the highest score obtained by users in all passed Learning Objects. Average grade If you choose this mode Moodle will calculate the average of all scores. Sum grade With this mode all the scores will be added. Go with the Sum Grade option based on the number of quizzes you have.I would definatley use the authoring tool to score this lesson. It may be easier to average the grades as well. You also get to choose how you handle returning students. You indicated highest grade recorded. The issue here is that if Moodle has issues communicating with a SCORM package then the grades may not get recorded properly. This brings me back to my first point. What authoring tool are your developers using? Let me know and I will try to help, Blaine

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM course scoring issues
ResponsesInList.Text: Chris, regarding number 2 in your reply. If you create a course+Lesson in Moodle then you can set pass rates. For example, you can create a lesson with questions that get graded. you can even create a quiz with the built-in quiz maker and set a required pass rate there as well. SCORM is designed to be completely self-contained. A lesson, quiz, resources, activities , etc. all zipped up. This is what makes it portable - reusable. So when you import a SCORM (add activity) it relies for the most part on the Learning Objectives/Rules settings in the published content. Definitely use the authoring tool to create these pass rates. Sounds like your SCORM may be proprietary to your other LMS(?). Meaning the same company that developed the content maintains the LMS? Not sure, but the more info you can get on the authoring tool the better off you will be in creating a solution. Let me know what you find, Blaine

ResponsesInList.Title: "Manifest not found" error - a solution!
ResponsesInList.Text: If anyone is getting this error when uploading SCORM files, then it may be that your files aren't being unzipped, which means Moodle can't see the imsmanifest. xml file. In which case, check the path to the unzip program on your server , under "Server>System Paths". Ours read: /usr/bin/uzip when it should be: /usr/bin/unzip I've had this problem for a while and couldn't find an answer until I tried to unzip some other files in Moodle and got a message saying: sh: /usr/bin/uzip: No such file or directory When I changed the path to the unzip program, all the SCORM files worked!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: cmi.core.total_time
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Juan, Actually for detailled statistics on SCORM content and usage I use SQL to query directly the db. This query can give you the data your are looking for SELECT mu.id, mu.firstname, mu.lastname, SEC_TO_TIME(SUM(TIME_TO_SEC(msst.value))) FROM mdl_user mu LEFT JOIN mdl_scorm_scoes_track msst ON mu.id= msst.userid WHERE msst.element = "cmi.core.total_time" GROUP BY mu.id Hope this helps Ciao Marco

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: cmi.core.total_time
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Juan Carlos, Yes I think it's possible. Try with this: SELECT dt.fina, dt.lana, dt.toti, ms.name, ms.course FROM( SELECT msst.scormid as courseid, mu.id, mu.firstname as fina, mu.lastname as lana, SEC_TO_TIME(SUM(TIME_TO_SEC(msst.value))) as toti FROM mdl_user mu LEFT JOIN mdl_scorm_scoes_track msst ON mu.id= msst.userid WHERE msst.element = "cmi.core.total_time" GROUP BY msst.scormid, mu.id ) as dt LEFT JOIN mdl_scorm ms ON dt.courseid =  ms.id Is what you was lookin for? ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What SCORM version is supported by Moodle 1.9?
ResponsesInList.Text: Mike, to say Moodle 1.9 is/is not SCORM compliant is tricky (okay, before I get inundated with emails let me explain). You can certainly display most SCORM presentations within Moodle. The problem seems to be a combination of things: Gradebook: reporting to Gradebook is a huge issue, just browse the SCORM forums to see how data is NOT getting into Gradebook. Check out what Bryan Williams over at Remote-Learner says about the work going on to fix this: http://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=91693 Display: I don't have a problem displaying any SCORM presentations I have created with two different authoring tools. However, there are issues with VML-objects and VML (Vector Markup Language) not being supported by FireFox . SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics - another vector format) could be the good alternative, but there are still problems with displaying inline SVG-objects in both Gecko-family and IE (according to what I have been told by the floks at CourseLab). I have a basic powerpoint presentation published to SCORM 1.2 with Pointecast Pro posted at the Blueprint2Safety site. Just a simple PPT with audio (not the best audio, but not a Moodle issue). You do have to create an account to view the lesson (for free of course, privacy ensured!). This is in flash format so you can see what it looks like. Bottom line is I can display SCORM well, Gradebook issues are being addressed. Moodle WILL overcome these issues because of the determination of the great support from the Moodle community! Hope this helps, Blaine

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM working in IE, not Firefox
ResponsesInList.Text: Okay, being code-challenged, i got an answer of this sort: It seems that FireFox has even more restrictions on cross- domain links with active content than IE - IE has too, but refers to domain names first, therefore in IE there is usually no or little problem. Also, please note, that some published content and authoring tools use specific IE features (so they may look not correct in FF). For example, AutoShapes are VML-objects and VML (Vector Markup Language) is not supported by FireFox (or i have been informed). SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics - another vector format) could be the good alternative, but there are still problems with displaying inline SVG-objects in both Gecko-family and IE. Therefore, if the choice is IE-only or nothing - we choose IE-only. Personally, I like FireFox, but, when it comes to active and dynamic content, all Gecko-based browsers are weaker than IE. That's just the fact

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: LArge SCORM file to be add to Course
ResponsesInList.Text: FTP the SCORM zip file to the directory moodledata/N , where moodledata is the value you specified for $CFG-> dataroot in config.php) N is the course number When you create the SCORM activity, you can browse to the file and select it.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: LArge SCORM file to be add to Course
ResponsesInList.Text: SCORM files need to go into the folder allocated to your course within your moodledata folder. The folder name will usually be a number that corresponds to the unique id number of your course in the moodle database . (E.g. 2, 3, etc) However, if your moodledata folder has been created outside the webserver folders (as is the recommended practice for improved file security) then you may not be able to reach it using FTP unless your browsing privileges extend to non-web directories. If this is a scenario you are likely to encounter often, have you looked into increasing the upload file limit to something more generous such as 10-16 meg instead?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: LArge SCORM file to be add to Course
ResponsesInList.Text: Here's how I do it: 1 – Upload the file to $:/moodle/uploaddata using your FTP client. 2 – While that’s happening, you can open your moodle and select ‘Courses’ >>> ‘Add/edit courses’ 3 – Select ‘Add new course’ 4 – Enter the course name, short code, a brief summary, and set your options. Save changes. 5 – Assign user roles Click the button in the bottom-centre - this takes you to the "Add SCORM/AICC" page 6 – Enter the course-name again, and the summary again then click ‘choose or upload a file’ which opens a pop-up. Opening this pop-up creates a new numbered directory on the server Close the pop-up without doing anything. 7 – Assuming the upload is complete, on your FTP client, move the newly uploaded zip file to the newly created numbered directory 8 – On your moodle click ‘Choose or upload a file’ again. This time, your zip file should be visible in your pop-up. Click ‘Choose’ and the pop-up closes, the filename of the zip file appears above the ‘Choose or upload a file’ button Select your options Click ‘Save changes’

ResponsesInList.Title: Firefox issues with SCORM = solution?
ResponsesInList.Text:
Because of the way FF treats Strings ( IE casts a result to the right type), Firefox doesn't always work with SCORM packages, ie. scores are not stored. I suggest the culprit is the code: 
```text
 elementmodel = element.replace(expression,'.n.');
```
 in the various datamodel files, for example there are 4 occurrences in scorm_12.js.php. Replacing this with 
```text
 elementmodel = String(element).replace(expression,'.n.');
```
 makes it "Firefox-compliant" This is the case for moodle 1.6 through 1.8. I suggest we make this change to the code, as it surely doesn't affect compatibility with IE.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM Module initial setup- Need Assistance
ResponsesInList.Text: You have a layered architecture. The bottom layer is LAMP, WAMP , MAMP , or whatever. Above this you have the learning management system (LMS) layer -- for example, Moodle, Blackboard etc.. SCORM sits above the LMS layer and does not depend in any way on the lower layers. So the correct question to ask is Which SCORM package should I download which is supported by the Moodle platform? Since Moodle is not yet fully compliant with SCORM 2004, I would recommend downloading a SCORM 1.2 package if one is available. But I may have misunderstood your question. If you are talking about the SCORM Conformance Test Suite , this is a a program you can use to test a given SCORM package for compliance with the standard. It only runs on Windows.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: LMSFinish just reloads the course
ResponsesInList.Text: I haven't worked with the SCORM API in a while, but as I recall, LMSFinish() simply terminates the current SCO and sends any unsent data back to the LMS. It does not terminate the SCORM package as a whole. In fact, I do not believe that SCORM has any such concept as "terminating a package." So when you click the exit button created by Lectora, you are telling it you are finished with the current SCO, and the logical action is to take you back to the initial page of the package, which (depending on your SCORM settings), could be either the content structure page or the first content page. Think about it: SCORM knows nothing about the context in which it is being played. It is completely self-contained. If it is being played in Moodle and you want to return to Moodle's main course page, click the Exit activity button to the right of the breadcrumb trail. This button is provided by Moodle , so it knows about the main course page and can take you there. Incidentally, if you press the Exit activity button while in a SCO, it will trigger a call to LMSFinish() so you don't have to worry about results for that SCO not being passed back to the LMS.

ResponsesInList.Text: Your version of Captivate is not likely to be the issue. I am able to successfully play and track Captivate 2 and 3 SCORM packages either zipped or unzipped in Moodle courses. But it cost me quite a lot of angst before I managed to crack this issue, especially on IIS . The issue with Captivate SCORMs not playing is usually caused by your web server setup. If you are using an Apache web server, try toggling the Server > HTTP > Use Slash Arguments setting. You may find that this solves your problem. If you are using Microsoft IIS, the solution is much more complicated and has to do with the inability of IIS to handle slashed arguments in Moodle's files.php page. There's actually quite a lot of information around about this issue on the SCORM forum. Use the Advanced Search to find posts in the SCORM forum that mention Captivate.  Here's a series of posts (mainly from me) that cover the technical axpects of what you may need to do if you are unfortunate enough to be stuck with IIS as your web server: http://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=80548 If you are lucky enough to have the option of using Apache, I would personally advise you to go that way. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SCORM /IMS won't load common.js base.css content.css
ResponsesInList.Text: Rodolfo, Try ticking or unticking the box at Admin > Server > HTTP > Use Slash Arguments and see if that helps. The problem is caused by the way Moodle uses the files.php page to serve up content out of the moodledata course files area. It seems to fool some web servers into thinking that the served files actually come from the same folder location as files.php itself. As a result, the browser goes looking for the linked files in that directory too, not in the original moodledata folder where they are actually located. This results in "page not found" or 404 errors. In most Apache server implementations, toggling the Slash Arguments setting does the trick. However, other web servers (such as IIS ) can require more drastic measures to overcome this issue, including using ISAPI Rewrite rules to fool the web server into submission. This issue affects most SCORM courses on IIS servers, and indeed any web page delivered from course files where a linked JS or CSS or SWF file is required for content to display properly. If toggling the slash arguments setting doesn't do the trick for you, search the forums here for references to similar issues with IIS and you will find lots of suggested workarounds. Cheers, Rod Ward

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: export in SCORM format
ResponsesInList.Text: Hey JB!, Let me add some more details why Moodle does not export its courses in SCORM format. First of all, SCORM is about self-paced content and evaluations, while a Moodle course is much, much than content and self-paced learning. So, if we export a Moodle course as SCORM, we will have to exclude all interaction tools keeping only content (resources) and -probably- quizzes. We will have to remove forums, assignment, workshops, choice tools. If we export Moodle quizzes and because SCORM does not include a teacher/tutor/mentor role we will have to remove essay questions. As you can see, we will be only exporting what we have added as a "Resource" (HTML pages, docs, pdfs & ppts) Second. A content to take full advantage of SCORM must include some piece of code to "talk" to servers back and forth storing and/or retreiving student/user's performance. Most of our content uploaded to our Moodle courses does not include this code, so it makes no sense to export our Resources as SCORM content. As you can see is not a good idea to export a Moodle course as SCORM, I think this will only gives us headaches than solutions. So, please go ahead with eXe, or with WebSoft CourseLab, great too, free, not opensource but free!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Scorm 1.8 Blank Screen
ResponsesInList.Text: One possible workaround is to increase upload file size. This is how you can do it For the most part, you can control the ability of uploading LARGE (>8mb files) by modifying your php.ini file. However, your modifications will likely go beyond if the "upload_max_filesize" variable is modified. Here's how to modify the php.ini to get an 11mb+ upload to function: upload_max_filesize = 20M ; DEFAULT is 2M max_execution_time = 300 ; DEFAULT is 30 [seconds] post_max_size = 12M ; DEFAULT is 8M You may also find it necessary to modify the "memory_limit" Resource Limit. In order to get a 3MB upload to work, you only have to modify the upload_max_filesize variable. However, file uploads may fail because of script timeouts (exceeding max_execution_time) if you've got a poor network connection between your client and server. Full info about increasing upload file size by this thread .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: importing a scorm module into moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: The usual reason for getting this error is that you (or the app that created your SCORM package) has zipped the folder containing all the files as well as the files inside that folder. For Moodle to find the imsmanifest.xml file it must be inside the zip file at the root level, i.e. not down another level inside a folder. If it unzips the SCORM and all it finds is a folder, it doesn't then know to look inside this folder for the manifest. It just tells you it can't find what it's looking for. So if this turns out to be the reason for your error, you can do one of two things: Unzip the SCORM package yourself somewhere and then dive inside the folder (to the level where you should be able to see the imsmanifest.xml), select all, and then create another zip archive to upload to Moodle. If the imsmanifest is at the root level, Moodle should be happy. Alternatively, you can use Moodle to unzip the SCORM package you have currently uploaded to your Course Files, and then just choose the imsmanifest.xml file directly. Either way it should work. If for any reason it still doesn't work, check the forum archives for threads about early versions of Moodle 1.7 and 1.8 that had a code bug preventing imsmanifest.xml from being found. However, if you are using the latest version of Moodle (1.8.3) I believe this has long since been fixed.

This is as per the suggestion of the following page - http://docs.moodle.org/en/Development:Working_with_the_Community To actually use the changes you will need to apply the patch to your existing scorm_13.js.php and locallib.php files. If you are running on a *nix machine it is as simple as this. From the command line cd to the folder that contains the patch and run 'patch locallib.php locallib.php_patch.txt' and 'patch scorm_13.js.php scorm_13.js.php_patch.txt' This will merge the changes into the files. You can now copy these files into the scorm module and it should work from there. For windows it is basically the same but you will probably need to download a patch program. ResponsesInList.Title: Survey results tracking in SCORM module
ResponsesInList.Text: Using Lectora v 2007 and Moodle 1.8, SCORM 1.2 I have created a SCORM module and successfully published it in my Moodle test system. The module includes a survey questionnaire and a one question test. The survey questionnaire includes multiple answer-multiple choice questions, short answer questions, and single-answer multiple choice questions. When I try out the course and answer all of the questions, not all of the answers show up in the Moodle tracking. I took a look at the underlying MySQL table where results are recorded and found that the multiple-answer questions are not tracked at all, if more than one answer is checked. I have just started working on putting the course into Lectora. There will be more tests. Is this a Moodle issue, a SCORM issue, or something else? In addition, the client will be using a different LMS from Moodle. Is it possible that the tracking behavior in another LMS will differ from Moodle, even though it is also SCORM compliant?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Survey results tracking in SCORM module
ResponsesInList.Text: Cyrelle, I think you will find that most people that have used SCORM and 'SCORM-compliant' systems of any flavour will tell you that it's never quite as simple as it is claimed to be. I can tell you that Moodle can definitely report SCORM data, but that sometimes you have to play with the settings in your editing tool, and/or in Moodle, to get everything playing nicely. Before faulting either Moodle or Lectora I would first check that your multiple answer questions are definitely set up to report their answers along with the other ones in the lesson . (In my tool of choice, Captivate, you have to tick a box on each question to make it report answers. Does Lectora have anything similar perhaps?) Your issue could also be something to do with the way that your Lectora-created SCORM package tries to communicate with Moodle's SCORM API. This communication is usually handled via Javascript .  There are several ways to configure the Javascript to work better with a given LMS. (The Moodle forums have some topics on this. Search for anything mentioning the SCORM API.) However, this usually means that the SCORM does or doesn't report, rather than that it fails to report a single type of question. Sadly, the fact that a SCORM works perfectly with one LMS does not guarantee that it will do so with another. And on a happier note, the fact that it fails to work with one you choose, is also no guarantee it won't work with the one your client wants to use. Welcome to the SCORM 'standard'. It's not quite as foolproof as we would all like...at least not just yet.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: In a SCRUM over SCORM
ResponsesInList.Text: Dan, Do your courses actually use sequencing and navigation rules? If not, you may be making life for yourself more complicated than is necessary. Sequencing (where the learner's path through the content is altered depending on previous actions) is a feature introduced in SCORM 2004. Earlier versions of SCORM didn't have it. But your courses don't need to actually use SCORM sequencing and navigation to be "SCORM compliant".  You just need to comply with SCORM rules for any features you DO actually make use of. If you are still struggling with the basics of SCORM, you may be wise just to shoot for compliance with SCORM 1.2 for now and be happy with that.  Version 1.2 isn't quite as complex, but it still gives you the ability to claim "SCORM compliance" (as long as you put 1.2 in the fine print...)

A Lesson may have several of these (Lecture, Reading, Forum, Quiz, and (possibly) a Simulation) We do not teach by altering content depending on previous actions. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: In a SCRUM over SCORM
ResponsesInList.Text: Dan, If, as you say above, it doesn't really matter in which order the student works through the material, then the extra features in the SCORM 2004 standard are probably overkill for your circumstance. If the tool that creates your SCORM package allows you to specify either SCORM 1.2 or 2004 as the output, try both and upload each package into Moodle and see which seems to give you the best results. I use Adobe Captivate to create animated tutorials for policies and procedures and software training. I find that Moodle and Captivate seem to work together quite well using SCORM 1.2, but so far I've not had much luck getting SCORM 2004 to behave and record scoring. SCORM is all about tracking learners. So how and where you use it also depends to a large extent on which elements of your course you need to track. If it turns out that you only really want to track what users are scoring in the Quiz part of your course, then that may be the only part you need to create as a SCORM package. If you want to know (and report on) whether or not your learners acccessed and completed all the reading as well, then you also need to include those items in your package as separate SCOs. So work out exactly what you need to track, then work out how you want those items presented to users. You could have each item as a single SCO SCORM package. Or you could have all of them in a multi-SCO SCORM package. Your choice. But before you go too far down the track, at least do some testing to make sure that your tool of choice will create SCORMs that Moodle will happily interact with first.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Completion tracking: OK. Scoring: not working
ResponsesInList.Text: Liam, First You may need to look at the way you've set up your SCORM when you authored it. I'm assuming that each of your questions in your final quiz have been set up to score a given number points each. You need to know what the maximum possible score is if a learner gets everything correct. (e.g If you have 11 questions worth 5 points each, then your max possible score is 55). Next, when you set up your SCORM in your Moodle course, you need to configure the way Moodle calculates the score. If you are after a typical percentage score in the gradebook, I suggest you set Grading Method to Highest Grade , then set Maximum Grade to match the maximum possible score  for that lesson . (In the example above this was 55. You will note that the Highest Grade drop-down list only goes up to 100, so your max score for any single SCORM is 100. I once ignored this and had a big final assessment with 36 questions all set to 10 points each. Needless to say, Moodle didn't know what to do with a maximum score of 360.) This should mean that Moodle now has enough information to calculate a percentage score for your lesson and can display correct percentage scores for users in the course Gradebook. But there are still lots of extra ways to tweak the display of scores. From your screenshot it appears that you haven't configured using the Advanced Features .  Try playing with the settings. For example, you can add Categories and assign a group of lessons to each one. This will break your scores up because Moodle will calculate a percentage score for each category, etc.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Page not found error when accessing scorm activity
ResponsesInList.Text: Carlos and Andre, SCORM packages typically have a bunch of files that interact in quite precise ways. It doesn't take much to throw a spanner in the works. Your problem could be something to do with the way your webserver is handling Moodle's calling of content from the moodledata course files folders. It passes arguments on the end of URLs in a certain way that can confuse the webserver.  This is where the spanner goes into the works and as a result, a SCORM package that plays perfectly elsewhere can suddenly stop working when you upload it to Moodle. Happily, if you are using Moodle with an Apache web server there's something easy you can try. Go to Admin > Server > HTTP > Use Slash Arguments and change the setting there from whatever it is at present. Most Apache servers need this setting to be ticked. Using this, I was able to get my Captivate SCORM 1.2s working perfectly on Apache. However, if you are using IIS as your web server, the fix is somewhat more complex and I'm just grappling with that situation myself at the moment.

ResponsesInList.Title: More than 10 objective per SCO
ResponsesInList.Text: I had a problem with a SCO that defined more than 10 objectives causing a javascript error when the cours launched, the LMSInitialize would fail, 9 or less objectives would work. I looked into the problem and found it.  It's in the scorm1_2.js.php file.  There is a loop on about line 134 that handles the 'cmi.objectives' elements. Basically there is an if statement in that loop that assumes the objectives will be in order (from 1 to N).  But becuase the element is stored as a string, the elements would be string ordered, so if there were 10 objectives the order would be 1,10,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. I replaced the code starting on line 130 with the following and it now handles N number of objectives per SCO: <?php $count = 0; $objectives = ''; $idArray = array(); //ADDED array to track the objectives already defined. foreach($userdata as $element => $value){ if (substr($element,0,14) == 'cmi.objectives') { preg_match('/.(\d+)./',$element,$matches); $element = preg_replace('/.(\d+)./',"_\$1.",$element); //COMMENTED OUT OLD IF STATEMENT //if ($matches[1] == $count) { //ADDED if statement to search the array of objectives already defined if( !(strlen(array_search($matches[1], $idArray)) > 0) ){ array_push($idArray, $matches[1]); //ADD the objective ID to the array $count++; $end = strpos($element,$matches[1])+strlen($matches[1]); $subelement = substr($element,0,$end); echo '    '.$subelement." = new Object();\n"; Just thought you guys should know.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: taking scorms more than once
ResponsesInList.Text: Mike, There's an obscure little setting inside Captivate's SCORM settings that you might check. It's to do with sending Resume data to the LMS . Resume data tells the LMS what interaction within a SCORM that the user reached at the time he terminated the lesson prematurely. If Resume data is sent to the LMS when the user terminates a lesson, when the learner attempts the SCORM again, it will reopen at the point where he finished last. From your description, this appears to be part of what is happening. You'll find this setting in Captivate Quiz Preferences > Reporting > Advanced > LMS Customization Settings > Never send Resume data This box is somewhat counter intuitive. If you tick the box, Captivate does NOT send Resume data to the LMS. (Which is a bit back-to-front to my way of thinking.) By default it is unticked, which means that Resume data DOES get sent and therefore the SCORM will respond accordingly when reopened. Another thing to check is what you have specified as the number of times the user can attempt the lesson. You can specify this within Captivate's Quiz Preferences > Reporting > Pass or Fail options. But if you set this to 1, it just means that the learner can only make one attempt to pass the quiz before reopening it again in another browser window. Conversely, you can set the Number of Attempts for an entire SCORM in Moodle's SCORM settings. I usually set this to greater than 1 to allow for any browser issues that might accidentally terminate a lesson mid-stream for a user. If you are getting the Review window appearing, it would seem that Moodle thinks the learner has used up all thier available attempts. Furthermore, for your SCORM scoring in Moodle to work with Captivate, you need to add up the points you've set for each quiz question inside Captivate and make sure this exactly matches what you set inside Moodle as your Maximum Grade number. You say yours is set to 100, probably because you think this is how Moodle will calculate a percentage, but it doesn't work that way. If your SCORM has a maximum possible score of 75 points, you have to set Moodle's Maximum Grade for that SCORM to 75. Then Moodle will correctly show scoring percentages for each learner. I've also found that it's not a good idea to have the total number of points in a SCORM add up to anything greater than 100 because this means you cannot set the Maximum Grade value high enough in Moodle. Something to watch out for if you have more than 10 questions in a SCORM because by default Captivate sets a quiz question to 10 points. Hope this helps your issue. Rod Ward

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: max_time_allowed
ResponsesInList.Text: The maxTimeAllowed xml variable in imsmanifest.xml appears to apply only to a SCO, not the entire SCORM that the SCO belongs to. The other variable mentioned in your post, time_limit_action also applies to the same object and is intended to trigger one of several actions; exit with a message, exit without a message, continue with message, continue without a message . If the tool you are using doesn't provide some user-friendly interface method of modifying these SCORM variables, you'd have to get into the xml code in imsmanifest.xml (using Notepad or a similar text editor) and modify it yourself. But this is not for the faint-hearted. You must get the time format exactly right and in exactly the right place. In Adobe Captivate, which I use, you have three places where you can set time limits. The highest level is for the SCORM package itself, but it's not so much a limit as an estimated time to complete the SCORM/course. If you set the Duration to say 1 hour and 35 minutes (under Quiz Preferences > Reporting > SCORM ) you'll see this code inside the imsmanifest: <educational> <typicallearningtime> <datetime> 1:35:00</datetime> </typicallearningtime> </educational> But that's set for the Course, not the SCO within the SCORM. Further down in the same Captivate dialog box, If you set the SCO variable for Time Limit to 15 minutes, you'll see this code in the imsmanifest for that SCO item:' <item identifier="MY_SCO" isvisible="true" identifierref="MY_SCO_RES"> <title>About Me</title> <adlcp:maxtimeallowed> 0:15:00</adlcp:maxtimeallowed> <adlcp:datafromlms></adlcp:datafromlms> <adlcp:masteryscore></adlcp:masteryscore> <adlcp:timelimitaction>exit,message</adlcp:timelimitaction> </item> Captivate also allows you to set a time limit on each individual quiz question/interaction you set up inside a lesson . But this doesn't affect the imsmanifest. It just means the interaction times out and prevents the learner from inputting an answer if they are too late. In Moodle, when you set up a SCORM, there's no setting available to modify or set a time limit on completion of the SCO. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to determine SCO identifier in manifest file?
ResponsesInList.Text: Nicolas, You need to develop some type of naming convention that gives you a fighting chance at being unique across multiple LMS servers. Your SCO identifier should ideally be meaningful enough to give you some guide as to the contents of the item. E.g. AboutLifeOnOtherPlanets If then you enhance uniqueness by appending a value to the beginning of your SCO identifier, it becomes more unlikely to be repeated by someone else. In practice this can be almost anything, but the longer it is, the less likely any other server will have one. E.g. If you append the year 2007 to the beginning of a SCO ID ( 2007_AboutLifeOnOtherPlanets ) there's still a chance someone else may have done the same. However, if you included the month so that it becomes 200709_AboutLifeOnOtherPlanets the likelihood reduces considerably, and then 20070905_AboutLifeOnOtherPlanets even less etc, etc. Alternatively, you could append your own name, a hexadecimal value, a 128bit encryption algorithm, or your favourite lotto numbers. Whatever takes your fancy. The longer the value, the lower the risk, but the more inconvenient when you type it in. My two cents worth. Rod Ward

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: index.html pointing to viewer.swf
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Couple of things you might check: Your URL in the second case has a backslash after the servername ( http://10200.companyname.com \ SCORMVIDEO/viewer.swf). Check to see if changing this to a forward slash helps. Check with your network geeks to find out if they've got some kind of packet filtering active on the network or the firewalls to prevent your video files from being played from that location. I've had similar problems at some sites where management wanted to stop employees from spending all day on UTube, so they deliberately disabled video files. You can check for this by trying to link directly to the video file from another web page with a normal hyperlink and see if the video will download as a file. If the server returns an error page saying you don't have 'permissions', then you can ask management if they can make an exception for your video files to be allowed. If the web server where the video file is now located happens to be IIS , you may need to get the server administrator to configure it to serve your video file type. By default, IIS 6.0 comes out of the box in 'lockdown' mode so that it is more secure. This means that it will only serve a very small number of specific filetypes (htm, html, css , js, etc) that are normally found on most static websites. Video files are definitely not on this list. So your webserver admin dude has to add the required files and their mimetypes to the configuration of IIS so that the server 'knows' it's supposed to serve them too. Hope this helps. Rod Ward

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Please tell me, Why SCORM?
ResponsesInList.Text: Samir, The SCORM (Sharable Content Object Reference Model) grew out of a need to have portability of content from one Learning Management System/Platform to another. Too often; a lot of time, effort, and money were invested in learning content just to have it become obsolete when your LMS provider went out of business or decided to go in a different technological direction. This was very prominent in contracts between content/LMS vendors and the United States Federal Government in the late 1990s. To help overcome this, the Department of Defense & White House Office of Science and Technology Policy for Advanced Distributed Learning banded together with business professionals and academia to move toward combining existing standards and best practices in the form of a model (i.e., SCORM). Since then, SCORM has been updated and has continued to adapt to increase communication between the LMS and learning content, add sequencing, and increased reusability and tagging of content (i.e., learning objects, resources, assets., etc.). Now, back to your original question; you may not need to convert to SCORM if you and your organization are happy with the functionality of your existing HTML courses and are secure that they will be supportable in the future.  If on the other hand, you would like to increase the integration and communication between your courses and LMS/LCMS, SCORM is a good choice. I personally have been developing under SCORM since it became available (I was a charter member of the Research Priorities Group of ADL).  While not a perfect solution, I believe SCORM is a very viable choice. NOTE: In theory, content developed under a particular SCORM version should be compatible with any LMS of the same SCORM version.  In practice, this is often not the case as some vendors use variations in the way they apply the model.  In other words, some are compliant while others are only conformant with the model. Good luck in your endeavor. V/R Les Amidon, Senior Learning Architect, Informs, Inc.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tárgy: Re: Please tell me, Why SCORM?
ResponsesInList.Text: Dokeos is a spin-off of Claroline, so I am not suprised that you can exchange courses between these two systems. It is - as far as I know - not possible to port a Dokeos course to Moodle or any other e-learning system.  (Even if you would only create Dokeos-courses in a learning-line-format, you still have to find a way to map that learning-line on the sections of Moodle.) I agree with you that the more compliant you try to be with SCORM, the more you cripple the educational integrated power of your own system: Most VLE's are supporting and monitoring multi-user- activities , SCORM can only handle single user activities. Moodle solves this by offering a hybrid solution: small SCORMS can have a place next to other multiuser-modules(=activities) in the sections of a course. a Big SCORM can take the place of the sections in a Moodle course, but if you plugin the OPTIONAL sidebar block, you can still offer your Moodle group activities in combination with this big SCORM course. SCORM expects that every VLE will follow the rules for information exchange in the SCORM-way and does not support web-services in a normal way: if your VLE does not, you can use the "envelop trick" to play the SCORM-package in your VLE: a good place to start a study on this subject is: http://www.ostyn.com/standards/scorm/samples/singleSCOminiRTEwrap.htm (and, by the way, also his papers about competences are interesting) When the Americans came with SCORM, we started in The Netherlands an Academic group called SIX to stop them, but the promised standard Learning Design (From the Valkenburg group, now called IMS/LD) is still a promiss and we must admit: SCORM is the only exchange format publishers are finally supporting.. We - as secondary education schools - are working together with other schools, NOT having Moodle. Seems that someone had patented them years ago and decided to successfully sue Mickeysoft for using them. IE was changed as a result to show an ugly border around any embedded objects like SWF files and movies, plus a message that says: "Click to activate this control. Dynamically writing in the tags via an abstracted linked js function takes away this message. Anyway...back to my issue.) By trial and error I found that if I put a document.write() function in the head of an HTM file inside Course Files, it works fine. If I put the same function into a JS file and link it to the HTM file then load both to Course Files it throws a javascript error and the function doesn't work. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Captivate 2 + Moodle 1.8 - do they talk?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Martin, If you production host site is running IIS 6.0 then I can't tell you how to get it to play Captivates that you upload into the Course Files area. I tried everything I knew and ran into brick walls at every turn. Captivate movies use an HTM page that calls a function in an external Javascript file to dynamically write HTML code into the web page which then loads the SWF (Flash) movie. There are good reasons why it takes this route and normally it would work anywhere.  It works perfectly for instance if you just upload all three files into your webserver and click the URL to the HTM page. However...in Moodle, the files.php page that calls up stuff out of the Course Files area seems to disorient the browser and then it can't find and load the other files (the JS and SWF) that are linked to the HTM page. After much frustration and experimentation, I discovered that the browser goes looking for the linked files in the same folder as files.php, not the folder in Course Files where the original HTM is sitting, and where you've loaded the JS and SWF files that belong to it. Now I stress that this queer behaviour only happens when you are using IIS 6, and it doesn't matter what setting you toggle for slash arguments in Moodle. As soon as I changed over to Apache as my web server, I had no problems playing Captivates from Course Files. It's not Captivate's fault. I created a test HTM file with a single linked JS file that wrote HELLO WORLD to the browser, and that wouldn't work either if they were both inside Course Files AND you were on IIS 6. But worked perfectly under Apache. If you are desperate, AND, you are not trying to get SCORM tracking working (which requires that the SCORM package is loaded into Course Files) then you can upload your Captivate files into a folder outside Moodle on your webserver and just use the option in Moodle to link topics to them. This means you set up a new Resource in your Moodle course for each Captivate movie, and then use the URL to the Captivate HTM file. This should work. If it was SCORM tracking of Captivates that you were after, my only solution to offer is to get onto Apache server instead.  As I said in my last post. I still hold out hope that someone can get Captivates in Course Files to work under IIS 6, but I sure couldn't. And I spent several days on it. Hope this helps. Rod

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Best approach for Flash Course?
ResponsesInList.Text: Create a Flash module with SCORM 1.2 turned on in the publishing settings. After you have the entire Flash module built and published with an html page, you will have to create a SCORM manifest file and package. This file communicates to Moodle and reports the scores back to the grade book. To make a SCORM package I use Dreamweaver with manifest maker 1.2 This is an add-in to Dreamweaver and allows you to set all the variables and point to the main Flash HTML page, which is considered a SCO. You have to tell Manifest maker what to launch. Once you have a package, create a zip file for it. Next, create a SCORM/AICC activity on a topic in a course or create a SCORM/AICC course. Upload the zip file, unzip the contents, go into the unzipped folder and find the IMSMANIFEST file and choose it. You'll have a few other settings to establish, like what window to launch it, scoring, etc... that is the basic process... Captivate 2 is great for creating Flash type modules and has SCORM manifest creation built-in with one step. Good luck and good SCORMing. Evan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Best approach for Flash Course?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Ali, A SCORM course has these parts: A manifest. This is a file called imasmanifest.xml. The manifest file describes your course to the LMS. The manifest has information about the title of the course, the description of the course, the number of SCOs and the name of the file to launch for each SCO. Manifest maker helps you make the manifest file. A package. A package is a zip file that contains the manifest and all of the files that run the course. One or more SCOs. A SCO is something that can be launched by the LMS. A SCO has to communicate with the LMS using the SCORM API Adapter. The SCORM API adapter is a JavaScript object named "API". The SCO has to find the object. The SCO then calls methods associated with that object to initialize communcation with the LMS, get/set SCORM data items and terminate the communication with the LMS.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: scorm url tracking
ResponsesInList.Text: It may be possible to have Moodle on one server and your content on another. The problem is in the way a SCORM course talks to a LMS. The course has to call a JavaScript function in a different browser window. The browser requires that HTML in both windows come from the same server. If they do not come from the same server, the browser will report an access violation. There are several possible work arounds that include: - making the content available on your web server as a virtual directory - using load balancers to make the course and Moodle appear to come from the same server - using JavaScript changes to modfy the domain of the HTML (this is increasingly difficut to do and very limited There is a white paper on the ADL site that descibes this problem (the cross-domain problem) in much greater detail.

ResponsesInList.Text: Large web sites need many servers to handle the load so they use load balancers to distribute the web traffic to multiple servers. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: scorm url tracking
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi (and thanks Leo for that note on the ADL white paper. It was very useful.) This may not be what you're looking for exactly, but thought I'd share how we're handling this issue. What we're doing is installing just enough content on the Moodle server to force the SCORM API to run on that server - then have all resources pulled from another (the 'content') server. On the Moodle server (this would be a customer's Moodle server - so could be any domain): a. the SCORM manifest b. the files (SCOs) in the resource list of the SCORM manifest -  for us, these are all PHP files (pretty simple, so shouldn't need modifications) that load javascript files -  but (see below) all the javascript files are on the other "content" server On our content server (our web server): a. all the javascript files referenced in the PHP files on the moodle server b. all other resources: images, sound files, etc. that are referenced by the javascript. This way the SCORM API instance is on the Moodle server, so there are no cross-domain issues. Positives: 1. no cross domain issues Negatives: 1. (for us) Internet, not intranet, performance. All resources (javascript, images, sound) have to download from our website before they run. However, once they are cached locally by the browser, performance is sweet. Internet performance is fine anyway, so not much of a sacrifice.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: PHP files not parsing when loaded by file.php
ResponsesInList.Text: Roberto already answered the question. A SCORM package cannot contain a php script. Here is Claude Ostyn's explanation in his book In the Eye of the SCORM Server-dependent content Many content developers would like to be able to claim SCORM conformance for content that is delivered through an active server, such as .php, .asp or .jsp pages. Obviously these are not files that can be included in the package, since they are generated on the fly. ... Since such content is not self-contained, it cannot be reliably archived or transported and it cannot be used offline without recreating the server functionality on the client machine. The content does not conform to the spirit of the SCORM because it is not portable and cannot be delivered by generic Web servers without installing some specific active components on the server. There is currently no standard way to specify such an installation.
